# University (self-governing body of teachers and students) (`university`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by codex_book, paper, charitable_endowment_waqf
- Core idea: Teachers and students form a legal corporation with a charter: it governs itself, elects its head, owns property, is exempt from local courts, sets a fixed curriculum and examines candidates for degrees that are recognised elsewhere. The corporate form is the invention. Learning no longer depends on one famous teacher or one patron, a degree certifies competence to strangers, and the body can defend itself against town and bishop by threatening to leave. Method: lecture on a set text, then public disputation in which a thesis is attacked and defended by argument.
- Pitfalls:
  - Expecting a modern research university: teaching dominated, but university scholars also made original contributions, including work on motion at medieval Oxford and Paris
  - Arguing about 'the first university' without a definition: Nalanda, al-Qarawiyyin, al-Azhar and Bologna are different kinds of institution
  - Believing medieval universities taught a flat earth: the standard textbook, Sacrobosco's Sphere (c. 1230), teaches a round one
  - Proposing free inquiry in theology or contradicting Aristotle in a formal disputation can end in a heresy charge; philosophical questions were debated 'hypothetically'
- History: china: 124 BC – Imperial Academy (Taixue), a state school for officials with tens of thousands of students by the 2nd c. AD; india: c. 5th c. AD – Nalanda, a Buddhist monastic centre of learning with entrance tests, thousands of residents and foreign students (Xuanzang, 7th c.); destroyed c. 1200; greece: c. 387 BC – Plato's Academy; philosophical schools as private associations; AD 425 imperial school at Constantinople with salaried chairs; islamic: 859 – al-Qarawiyyin mosque in Fez founded (its status as a 'university' from that date is disputed); c. 970 al-Azhar; 1067 opening of the Nizamiyya madrasa in Baghdad, endowed colleges of law granting personal licences to teach (ijaza); africa: 14th–16th c. – Sankore and other mosque schools of Timbuktu; europe: c. 1088 (traditional date) – Bologna's law schools, organised as a student corporation in the late 12th c.; c. 1150–1215 Paris, a masters' corporation; Oxford by 1167; 1810 Berlin, Humboldt's union of teaching and research; americas: 1551 – royal charters for universities in Lima and Mexico City; 1636 Harvard College
- Read:
  - Hilde de Ridder-Symoens (ed.), A History of the University in Europe, vol. 1: Universities in the Middle Ages (1992)
  - George Makdisi, The Rise of Colleges: Institutions of Learning in Islam and the West (1981)
